questions.stem: Which sentence describes the **climate** of a place?
options: It is very windy at school this afternoon.
Sylhet gets a lot of rain every year.
Tomorrow morning will be foggy in Dhaka.
It rained heavily here all night last night.
questions.explanation: Climate is the usual weather of a place over many years. The other sentences describe the weather on one day, which can change in a few hours.

questions.stem: Sort these sentences into weather and climate.
items: It is very windy this afternoon.
Sylhet gets a lot of rain every year.
Bangladesh has a monsoon season every year.
Winters in Dhaka are cool and dry.
questions.explanation: Weather is what the air is like today or this week. Climate is the usual weather of a place, worked out from many years of measurements.

questions.stem: Climate is the usual weather of a place, worked out from many ___ of measurements.
questions.explanation: Climate is found by measuring the weather for many years, usually 30.

questions.stem: Match each weather instrument to what it measures.
questions.explanation: A thermometer measures temperature in °C and a rain gauge measures rain in mm. The wind vane shows direction, the anemometer shows speed, and the barometer measures air pressure.

questions.stem: Match each season in Bangladesh to its months (about).
questions.explanation: Summer is very hot with sudden storms. The monsoon is warm and very wet. Winter is cool and dry with foggy mornings.

questions.stem: Weather and climate can change non-living things too: heavy rain can make rivers flood.
questions.explanation: Weather and climate affect living things (rice is planted when the monsoon rains come) and non-living things (rivers flood, and heat and rain slowly break up rocks and roads).

questions.stem: Why is the air near the ceiling of a room warmer than the air near the floor?
options: Warm air rises to the ceiling.
Warm air sinks to the floor.
The ceiling gives out heat.
Heat cannot reach the floor.
questions.explanation: When air is warmed it spreads out, becomes lighter and rises. Cooler air stays lower down.

questions.stem: Put the steps in order to show how a sea breeze forms.
sequence: The Sun warms the land faster than the sea.
The warm air over the land rises.
Cooler air from the sea moves in to take its place.
This moving air is a sea breeze.
questions.explanation: Wind is moving air. On a sunny day the land warms faster than the water, warm air rises over the land and cool air blows in from the sea.

questions.stem: Which places are likely to be the warmest at noon? Choose all that are right.
options: a dark tin roof in direct sunshine
a dark road in direct sunshine
under a big shady tree
beside a pond in the shade
questions.explanation: It is warmest in direct sunshine, especially on dark surfaces. It is coolest in the shade of trees and near water.

questions.stem: A thermometer for measuring the air temperature should be kept in the ___.
questions.explanation: In direct sunshine a thermometer shows the temperature of the sunshine, not of the air. Keep it in the shade, about 1.5 m above the ground.

questions.stem: A thermometer left in direct sunshine shows the true temperature of the air.
questions.explanation: In direct sunshine the thermometer heats up and shows the temperature of the sunshine, not the air. It should be kept in the shade.

questions.stem: Why do many old houses in Bangladesh have small openings high up in the walls?
questions.model_answer: Warm air rises and escapes through the high openings, and cooler air comes in lower down, keeping the house cool.
questions.explanation: Warm air rises. The high openings let it out, and cooler air flows in lower down to take its place.

questions.stem: What does a barometer measure?
options: rainfall
air pressure
wind direction
temperature
questions.explanation: A barometer measures air pressure. Falling pressure often means a storm is coming.

questions.stem: White, puffy clouds in a blue sky usually mean…
options: a storm is coming
heavy rain is on the way
fine weather
a cyclone is near
questions.explanation: White, puffy clouds mean fine weather. Dark grey clouds hold more water and often bring rain.

questions.stem: Which clues can tell you that a storm may be coming? Choose all that are right.
options: the barometer is falling
tall dark clouds are growing
the wind changes direction
a clear blue sky with a few thin white clouds
calm air and no clouds at all
questions.explanation: Falling pressure, tall dark clouds and a change of wind direction can all mean the weather is about to change.

questions.stem: Look at the weather instruments. Match each letter to its name.
questions.image_alt: Five weather instruments lettered A to E.
questions.explanation: A is a thermometer, B a rain gauge, C a wind vane, D an anemometer and E a barometer.

questions.stem: Which letter shows the white, puffy cloud that usually comes with fine weather?
options: A
B
C
D
questions.explanation: A is a cumulus cloud: white and puffy, a sign of fine weather. D is a tall cumulonimbus that can bring thunderstorms.

questions.stem: Look at the clouds. Match each letter to the name of the cloud.
questions.explanation: Cumulus clouds are puffy, stratus clouds form flat grey layers, cirrus clouds are thin and wispy, and cumulonimbus clouds are tall and bring thunderstorms.

questions.stem: Look at the sea breeze picture. In the daytime, which way does the cool air move near the ground?
questions.image_alt: Daytime sea breeze: warm air rises over the land and cooler air moves in from the sea.
options: from the land to the sea
straight up into the sky
straight down into the sea
from the sea to the land
questions.explanation: The land warms faster than the sea, so warm air rises over the land and cooler air moves in from the sea to take its place.

questions.stem: Sort these weather pictures into fine weather and wet or stormy weather.
questions.explanation: A bright sun and a few small clouds mean fine weather. Rain clouds, thunder clouds and cyclones bring wet or stormy weather.

questions.stem: Rina's class sets up a weather station. Where should they keep the thermometer to measure the air temperature?
options: on the tin roof of the shed in the sun
on the hot concrete in the sunshine
in the shade, about 1.5 m above the ground
inside a closed cupboard
questions.explanation: The air temperature should be measured in the shade, away from heat from the ground and the Sun. A tin roof or concrete in the sun would read much too high.

questions.stem: On a hot afternoon, Joy wants to cool her room. It has one window near the floor and one near the ceiling. What should she do?
options: Open only the low window.
Open both windows.
Open only the high window.
Close both windows.
questions.explanation: Cool air comes in through the low window and warm air rises out through the high window, so opening both keeps the air moving.

questions.stem: Tomorrow is Sports Day. This afternoon the barometer is falling, the wind has changed direction and tall dark clouds are growing. What is the best forecast?
options: A storm with heavy rain is likely.
Hot, dry and sunny weather is likely.
Calm, clear weather is likely.
Cold, foggy weather is likely.
questions.explanation: Falling pressure, a change of wind direction and tall dark (cumulonimbus) clouds are signs of a storm.

questions.stem: A haor farmer hears a flash flood warning on the radio. It is better to wait until the rice is completely ripe before harvesting.
questions.explanation: Slightly unripe rice still gives some food and money, but a flash flood would destroy all of it. Farmers should harvest early.

questions.stem: Why do farmers in Bangladesh plant rice when the monsoon rains arrive?
options: Rice grows best in cold dry weather.
Rice needs a lot of water to grow.
Rain keeps birds away from the rice.
The monsoon makes the soil harder.
questions.explanation: Weather and climate affect living things. The monsoon brings the water that rice plants need.

questions.stem: Class 4A measured the rainfall each morning for five days: 0 mm, 2 mm, 10 mm, 25 mm and 30 mm. What was the total rainfall?
options: 57 mm
67 mm
77 mm
87 mm

questions.stem: Class 4A recorded the weather at 9 a.m. in June. Rain (mm): Sun 0, Mon 2, Tue 10, Wed 25, Thu 30. Pressure: steady, falling, falling, falling, low. On Thursday the clouds were dark and tall and the wind blew from the south-east, from the sea. Which forecast for Friday is best supported?
options: Dry and sunny, because Sunday was dry.
Dry, because the wind comes from the sea.
Wet again, because the rain is increasing and the pressure is low.
Cold and snowy, because the temperature is falling.
questions.explanation: A forecast uses trends. Rainfall has gone up every day, the pressure is low and the clouds are dark and tall, so more rain is likely.

questions.stem: A flood forecast for the hills near a haor gives the rain for the next five days as 5 mm, 10 mm, 60 mm, 120 mm and 80 mm (example values). What is the best advice for the farmers?
options: Wait until day 5, then harvest everything.
Harvest only on day 4, when the rice is driest.
Do nothing, because the rain amounts are small.
Harvest on days 1 and 2, before the heavy rain starts.
questions.explanation: The heavy rain begins on day 3 and a flash flood could come soon after. Harvesting early saves most of the crop.

questions.stem: Explain how wind is made. Use the words warm, rises and cool.
questions.model_answer: The Sun warms the ground, which warms the air above it. Warm air rises and cooler air moves in to take its place. This moving air is wind.
questions.explanation: Wind is air moving from a cooler place to take the place of warm air that has risen.

questions.stem: A class measured the temperature at 9 o'clock every morning for a week. Why did they measure at the same time each day?
questions.model_answer: So the results can be compared fairly, because the temperature changes during the day.
questions.explanation: The temperature rises and falls through the day, so measuring at different times would make the results unfair to compare.
